entries.title: Galatians 3:13 and Deuteronomy 21:23
entries.content:
Paul says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, and he backs this with a quotation: cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree. Set beside Deuteronomy 21:23, the quotation has been reshaped.

In Deuteronomy the rule concerns a man who has been put to death for a crime and whose body is then hung up for display. It must not stay up overnight but be buried the same day, because a hanged man is cursed by God and leaving him would defile the land. Paul leaves out the words “by God”, turns a rule about one executed criminal into a statement about everyone, and uses it to prove something the passage never discusses. Deuteronomy says nothing about atonement, and the curse it names falls on the man for his own crime.

his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.

Deuteronomy 21:23

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—

Galatians 3:13

entries.title: Galatians 3:10 and Deuteronomy 27:26
entries.content:
Paul quotes Moses to show that everyone who relies on the works of the law is under a curse: cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, and do them. The wording is longer than Deuteronomy 27:26, which curses anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.

Paul then argues that nobody can keep it all, so the law can only condemn. But Deuteronomy does not take that view of its own commandments. A few chapters later Moses tells Israel that the commandment is not too hard for them and not far off (Deuteronomy 30:11), and chapter 28 opens with blessings for those who obey. The curse of Deuteronomy 27 is the penalty for a people who choose to disobey, not a verdict that obedience is impossible.

“‘Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.’ And all the people shall say, ‘Amen.’

Deuteronomy 27:26

“For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.

Deuteronomy 30:11

For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”

Galatians 3:10

entries.title: Galatians 3:16 and Genesis 13:15
entries.content:
Paul builds an argument on a single grammatical point. The promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, and Scripture does not say offsprings, as of many, but offspring, as of one, who is Christ.

In Genesis the word is a collective singular, just as in English. Genesis 13:15-16 promises the land to Abraham’s offspring and in the next breath says that his offspring will be as numerous as the dust of the earth, which cannot be one person. Genesis 22:17 likewise has the offspring as many as the stars. Paul’s reading makes the word mean something the author plainly did not intend.

for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.

Genesis 13:15

I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted.

Genesis 13:16

Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.

Galatians 3:16

entries.title: Galatians 3:11 and Habakkuk 2:4
entries.content:
Paul quotes Habakkuk to prove that no one is justified before God by the law, because the righteous shall live by faith. In the ESV, Habakkuk says the righteous shall live by his faith.

The prophet is answering a complaint about injustice. The proud person is not upright, but the righteous person will stay alive through his own steadfast loyalty while he waits for the vision to come. The word can mean faithfulness as well as faith. Paul drops the “his”, sets the word against the law, and draws a contrast the verse does not make.

“Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith.

Habakkuk 2:4

Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”

Galatians 3:11

entries.title: Galatians 3:17 and Exodus 12:40
entries.content:
Paul says that the law, which came 430 years after the promise to Abraham, cannot cancel that earlier promise. The figure of 430 years matches one given in Exodus.

In Exodus 12:40 the 430 years is the length of time the people of Israel lived in Egypt, and Genesis 15:13 gives a round 400 years for their stay and affliction there. Neither figure measures the time between Abraham and Sinai. Paul uses a number the text gives for one span of time as though it measured another.

The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years.

Exodus 12:40

Then the LORD said to Abram, “Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years.

Genesis 15:13

This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.

Galatians 3:17

entries.title: Romans 3:10 and Psalm 14:1
entries.content:
In Romans 3:10-12 Paul proves that all humankind is under sin with the words “None is righteous, no, not one”, and presents them as Scripture. They are not a single quotation: the words come from Psalm 14:1-3 (repeated in Psalm 53) and are joined to lines from other psalms and from Isaiah.

Psalm 14 itself is about the fool who says in his heart that there is no God. The same psalm says in verse 5 that God is with the generation of the righteous, so the psalmist knows that righteous people exist. Paul takes a description of the wicked as a group and turns it into a statement about every human being.

The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good.

Psalm 14:1

There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous.

Psalm 14:5

as it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one;

Romans 3:10

entries.title: Romans 9:25 and Hosea 2:23
entries.content:
Paul quotes Hosea to show that God calls Gentiles as well as Jews: I will call ‘Not my people’ ‘My people’. In Hosea the words are about Israel.

Hosea’s children are named Not My People and No Mercy as a sign of the northern kingdom’s rejection, and the promises of Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 are that Israel itself will be restored and numbered like the sand of the sea. The people called Not My People are Israelites. Paul moves a promise about the restoration of Israel to the Gentiles.

Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or numbered. And in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” it shall be said to them, “Children of the living God.”

Hosea 1:10

and I will sow her for myself in the land. And I will have mercy on No Mercy, and I will say to Not My People, ‘You are my people’; and he shall say, ‘You are my God.’”

Hosea 2:23

As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved.’”

Romans 9:25

entries.title: Romans 10:6 and Deuteronomy 30:12
entries.content:
Paul says the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this: do not say in your heart, who will ascend into heaven, that is, to bring Christ down. He is quoting Deuteronomy 30, but with a different subject.

In Moses’ speech the commandment is not in heaven, so that Israel has to ask who will go up and get it. The word is very near, in the mouth and in the heart, so that you can do it (Deuteronomy 30:14). The word is the law. Paul replaces it with Christ, and stops short of the last words, so that you can do it, which would contradict his argument that the law cannot be kept.

“For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.

Deuteronomy 30:11

But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.

Deuteronomy 30:14

But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

Romans 10:6

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 9:9 and Deuteronomy 25:4
entries.content:
Paul cites the law of Moses, you shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain, and then asks: is it for oxen that God is concerned? He says the law was written entirely for our sake, to defend the right of the apostle to be paid.

Deuteronomy 25:4 is one of several rules about fair treatment. It is about the animal, and the rest of the Law shows the same concern, as does Proverbs 12:10, which says that the righteous person has regard for the life of his beast. Paul’s question denies the plain sense of the rule in order to apply it to something else.

“You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.

Deuteronomy 25:4

Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel.

Proverbs 12:10

For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned?

1 Corinthians 9:9

entries.title: Ephesians 4:8 and Psalm 68:18
entries.content:
Ephesians quotes Psalm 68:18 as saying that when he ascended on high he led a host of captives and gave gifts to men. The psalm says the opposite about the gifts.

The ESV of Psalm 68:18 has God ascending on high and receiving gifts among men, a victory procession in which tribute is collected from the conquered. Ephesians says he gave gifts to men. The verb has been reversed, and the change is what makes the verse useful to the argument about gifts to the church.

You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.

Psalm 68:18

Therefore it says, “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.”

Ephesians 4:8

entries.title: Hebrews 10:5 and Psalm 40:6
entries.content:
Hebrews 10:5 has Christ say, on coming into the world, that God desired no sacrifice but had prepared a body for him. The words are taken from Psalm 40:6.

The Hebrew text behind the ESV of Psalm 40:6 says that God has given the psalmist an open ear, literally that ears have been dug for him. The wording of Hebrews, a body you have prepared for me, matches an ancient Greek translation of the psalm and not the Hebrew. The argument in Hebrews 10:10, that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, depends on the word “body”, which the Hebrew psalm does not have. In the psalm the speaker is David, describing his own obedience.

In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required.

Psalm 40:6

Then I said, “Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me:

Psalm 40:7

Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;

Hebrews 10:5

entries.title: Acts 7:14 and Genesis 46:27
entries.content:
Stephen’s speech to the council in Acts 7 retells the history of Israel and disagrees with Genesis in two places.

First, in Acts 7:14 Joseph sends for his father Jacob and his family, seventy-five persons in all. Genesis 46:27 counts seventy. Second, Acts 7:16 says that Jacob’s family were buried at Shechem in the tomb Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor. In Genesis, Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and it was Jacob who bought a piece of land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19), where Joseph’s bones were later buried (Joshua 24:32). Stephen’s version merges two purchases made by two different men.

And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.

Genesis 46:27

So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over

Genesis 23:17

And from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, he bought for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land on which he had pitched his tent.

Genesis 33:19

As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph.

Joshua 24:32

And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all.

Acts 7:14

and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

Acts 7:16

entries.title: Luke 3:36 and Genesis 11:12
entries.content:
Luke’s genealogy of Jesus lists a man named Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah. Genesis 11:12-13 has no one between them: Arpachshad fathers Shelah.

The extra name is found in the ancient Greek translation of Genesis and not in the Hebrew text, so Luke’s list follows a different version of the genealogy than the Hebrew Bible. The count of generations from Adam to Abraham therefore differs between the two books.

When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he fathered Shelah.

Genesis 11:12

And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

Genesis 11:13

the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech,

Luke 3:36

entries.title: Hebrews 11:21 and Genesis 47:31
entries.content:
Hebrews says that by faith Jacob, when dying, worshiped, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. Genesis describes the same scene differently.

In Genesis 47:31 Israel bows himself upon the head of his bed. The Hebrew words for bed and staff are written with the same consonants and differ only in their vowels, and Hebrews follows the Greek translation, which read the word as staff. The story is the same, but the object Jacob leaned on is not.

And he said, “Swear to me”; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed.

Genesis 47:31

By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff.

Hebrews 11:21

entries.title: Matthew 2:15 and Hosea 11:1
entries.content:
Matthew says that Joseph took the child to Egypt and stayed there until Herod died, so that what the Lord had spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: out of Egypt I called my son.

In Hosea the words look back on the exodus. Israel is the son, and the very next verse says that the more he was called, the more he went away, sacrificing to the Baals. The sentence is a statement about the past, not a prediction, and it concerns the nation. Matthew treats it as a prophecy about Jesus.

When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.

Hosea 11:1

The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols.

Hosea 11:2

entries.title: Hosea 11:1 and Matthew 2:15
entries.content:
Matthew says that Joseph took the child to Egypt and stayed there until Herod died, so that what the Lord had spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: out of Egypt I called my son.

In Hosea the words look back on the exodus. Israel is the son, and the very next verse says that the more he was called, the more he went away, sacrificing to the Baals. The sentence is a statement about the past, not a prediction, and it concerns the nation. Matthew treats it as a prophecy about Jesus.

When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.

Hosea 11:1

The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols.

and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

entries.title: Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14
entries.content:
Matthew explains the birth of Jesus as the fulfilment of what the Lord spoke by the prophet: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel.

Isaiah gives this sign to King Ahaz, who is afraid of the kings of Syria and Israel marching against him. The child is a sign for Ahaz in his own time, and before he is old enough to tell right from wrong, the land of the two kings Ahaz dreads will be deserted (Isaiah 7:16). The Hebrew word translated virgin in the ESV is a general word for a young woman of marriageable age. Whatever its sense, the sign was given to Ahaz and answered within a few years, long before the birth of Jesus.

Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

Isaiah 7:14

He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good.

Isaiah 7:15

For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted.

Isaiah 7:16

“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us).

entries.title: Matthew 27:9 and Zechariah 11:12
entries.content:
Matthew says that the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah. No such passage is found in Jeremiah.

The thirty pieces of silver, cast into the house of the LORD for the potter, are in Zechariah 11:12-13. entries.title: Mark 1:2 and Malachi 3:1
entries.content:
Mark opens his Gospel with the words, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet, and then gives two quotations joined into one.

The first, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, is not in Isaiah. It comes from Malachi 3:1, where God says he will send his messenger to prepare the way before me, and in Mark the pronoun has been changed from me to you. entries.title: Mark 2:26 and 1 Samuel 21:1
entries.content:
Defending his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus recalls how David entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence.

In the story David receives the bread from the priest Ahimelech at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1-6). Abiathar was Ahimelech’s son, who escaped when Saul had the priests killed and only then joined David (1 Samuel 22:20). The name in Mark is wrong for the event he describes.

Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no one with you?”

So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away.

1 Samuel 21:6

But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.

how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?”

entries.title: Matthew 23:35 and 2 Chronicles 24:20
entries.content:
Jesus warns that on the leaders will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom they murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

The last murder in the Hebrew Bible, whose books end with Chronicles, is that of Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, who was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20-21). The prophet Zechariah, whose book begins at Zechariah 1:1, was the son of Berechiah, and the Bible does not record that he was murdered. The father’s name in the saying belongs to a different man.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you break the commandments of the LORD, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you.’”

2 Chronicles 24:20

But they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD.

2 Chronicles 24:21

In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,

Zechariah 1:1

so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

entries.title: Matthew 12:40 and Jonah 1:17
entries.content:
Asked for a sign, Jesus answers that no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.

Jonah 1:17 does say three days and three nights. In the Gospels, however, Jesus is crucified on a Friday and found risen early on Sunday, which is part of one day, a full night and a day, and part of another. The same Gospels say that he rose on the third day. The comparison with Jonah, as worded in Matthew, does not match the period the Gospels describe.

And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

Jonah 1:17

For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.

entries.title: Luke 4:18 and Isaiah 61:1
entries.content:
In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads from the scroll of Isaiah and says that the passage is fulfilled in their hearing. What Luke records him reading is not the text of Isaiah 61.

Isaiah 61:1-2 speaks of proclaiming liberty to the captives and the opening of the prison to those who are bound, and goes on to the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of vengeance of our God. Luke’s version adds recovery of sight to the blind and setting at liberty those who are oppressed, which echoes Isaiah 58:6, and he stops before the day of vengeance. The passage read is stitched together from more than one place in the book.

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound;

Isaiah 61:1

to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;

Isaiah 61:2

“Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?

Isaiah 58:6

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed,

entries.title: Matthew 15:8 and Isaiah 29:13
entries.content:
Jesus tells the Pharisees that Isaiah prophesied rightly of them: in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.

The ESV of Isaiah 29:13 says that the people’s fear of God is a commandment taught by men. In the Hebrew their worship is not called vain; the complaint is that their reverence has become a memorised human rule. The wording Jesus uses, in vain do they worship, follows the ancient Greek translation and not the Hebrew, and the point about teaching human doctrines depends on that reading.

And the Lord said: “Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men,

Isaiah 29:13

“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;

entries.title: Matthew 5:43 and Leviticus 19:18
entries.content:
In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says: you have heard that it was said, you shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you, love your enemies.

The first half is in the law: Leviticus 19:18 tells Israel to love their neighbour as themselves. The second half, hate your enemy, is not in the law anywhere. Leviticus 19:17 forbids hating a brother in the heart, and Exodus 23:4 commands returning an enemy’s lost ox or donkey. The saying Jesus corrects is a popular gloss on the commandment, not the commandment itself.

“You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him.

Leviticus 19:17

You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.

Leviticus 19:18

“If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him.

Exodus 23:4

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’

Matthew 5:43

entries.title: Mark 12:29 and Deuteronomy 6:4
entries.content:
Asked which commandment is the most important of all, Jesus answers with the Shema: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.

Jesus puts the oneness of God first, quoting Deuteronomy 6:4-5 as the greatest commandment. The scribe repeats it back in Mark 12:32, saying that God is one and there is no other besides him, and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom of God. In answering the question the teacher takes his place among those who hear and obey that commandment, and says nothing about himself.

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.

Deuteronomy 6:4

You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.

Deuteronomy 6:5

Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.

Mark 12:29

And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him.

Mark 12:32

entries.title: John 17:3 and Isaiah 45:5
entries.content:
In his prayer in John 17, Jesus addresses the Father as the only true God and speaks of himself as the one whom the Father has sent.

The words match the claim made throughout the Hebrew Bible. The LORD says in Isaiah 45:5, I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God, and Deuteronomy 4:35 says that the LORD is God and there is no other besides him. Jesus’ own prayer keeps the line between God who sends and the one who is sent.

I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me,

Isaiah 45:5

To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him.

Deuteronomy 4:35

And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

John 17:3

entries.title: John 10:34 and Psalm 82:6
entries.content:
When the Jews pick up stones for making himself God, Jesus answers from the law: is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? He argues that if Scripture calls those to whom the word of God came gods, he cannot be accused of blasphemy for saying he is the Son of God.

The line is from Psalm 82:6, where God stands in the council of the gods to judge them, and the “gods” are rulers and judges of the people, who will die like men (Psalm 82:7). Jesus’ reply uses the word god in the same loose sense, as a title for a human agent of God. Exodus 7:1, where God makes Moses like God to Pharaoh, uses it in the same way.

I said, “You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you;

Psalm 82:6

nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince.”

Psalm 82:7

Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’?

John 10:34

entries.title: Matthew 4:10 and Deuteronomy 6:13
entries.content:
Each time the devil tempts him in the wilderness, Jesus answers with a verse from Deuteronomy. The last answer is you shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.

The three answers come from Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13. In Deuteronomy 6:13 the command is to fear the LORD your God, serve him, and swear by his name. Matthew’s version replaces fear with worship and adds only. The sense is carried across, but the word “only”, which carries the weight in Matthew, is not in the verse he quotes.

It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.

Deuteronomy 6:13

And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Deuteronomy 8:3

“You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.

Deuteronomy 6:16

Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, “‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’”

Matthew 4:10

And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Deuteronomy 8:3

“You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.

entries.title: Matthew 22:44 and Psalm 110:1
entries.content:
Jesus asks the Pharisees whose son the Christ is, and they answer, the son of David. He asks how David, by the Spirit, then calls him Lord, quoting Psalm 110:1: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.

In the Hebrew of the psalm the first “Lord” is the divine name, and the second is a different word, adoni, my lord, an ordinary title of respect for a king or master that is used of men all over the Bible. The ESV marks the difference by spelling the first in capitals. The argument that the second Lord must be more than David’s son rests on the English and Greek, in which both words look alike.

The LORD says to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.”

Psalm 110:1

“‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”’?

Matthew 22:44

entries.title: Acts 13:33 and Psalm 2:7
entries.content:
Paul preaching in Antioch says that God has fulfilled the promise by raising Jesus, as it is written in the second psalm: you are my Son, today I have begotten you.

Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm. God has set his king on Zion, his holy hill (verse 6), and the declaration in verse 7 is made to that king on the day of his enthronement. 2 Samuel 7:14, where God says of David’s son that he will be to him a father and the king a son, uses the same language of adoption for the king of Israel. Applying the verse to the resurrection moves a royal formula into a different setting.

“As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill.”

Psalm 2:6

I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.

Psalm 2:7

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men,

2 Samuel 7:14

this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, “‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’

Acts 13:33

entries.title: Matthew 5:17 and Deuteronomy 4:2
entries.content:
Jesus says that he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfil them, and that until heaven and earth pass away not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.

This is consistent with Deuteronomy 4:2, which says that nothing is to be added to what God commands and nothing taken away, so that the commandments are kept. It does not fit what Paul teaches elsewhere about the same law. Paul says that Christ became a curse to redeem from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13), that those who accept circumcision must keep the whole law (Galatians 5:3), and that Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4). Set against the saying of Jesus, the teaching of Paul on the law looks like a different position.

You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.

Deuteronomy 4:2

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.

Matthew 5:17

For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.

Matthew 5:18

entries.title: Matthew 19:17 and Leviticus 18:5
entries.content:
A man asks Jesus what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Jesus answers that if he wants to enter life, he should keep the commandments, and then names several of them.

The answer follows Leviticus 18:5, where God says that the one who keeps his statutes and rules shall live by them. Paul quotes the same verse in Galatians 3:12 to prove the opposite point, that the law does not rest on faith, so whoever does the works of the law must live by them. In the Gospel, obedience to the commandments is the road to life, and Paul turns the same verse against it.

You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.

Leviticus 18:5

And he said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments.”

Matthew 19:17

But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”

Galatians 3:12
